title: Mapping summer heat across neighborhood blocks
abstract: Mobile temperature surveys measured summer heat along residential streets. The analysis compared tree canopy and shade with afternoon surface temperature to identify blocks with the greatest heat exposure.

title: Street tree canopy and pedestrian heat exposure
abstract: Street tree canopy was mapped along pedestrian routes using aerial imagery. Temperature sensors recorded heat exposure under shade and in open street segments during three summer sampling periods.

title: Cooling patterns near small urban parks
abstract: Temperature transects around urban parks measured how cooling varied with tree canopy and street orientation. The study examined whether park shade extended into adjacent residential blocks during summer heat events.

title: Shade access at neighborhood bus stops
abstract: Field observations at bus stops recorded tree canopy and shelter shade during summer afternoons. Temperature readings were paired with pedestrian wait times to estimate heat exposure along transit routes.

title: Nighttime heat retention in dense street corridors
abstract: Fixed temperature sensors captured overnight cooling in street corridors with different pavement and building cover. The analysis linked daytime shade and surface materials to neighborhood heat retention.

title: Rain gardens and runoff from residential streets
abstract: A paired monitoring design estimated stormwater runoff from residential streets with and without rain gardens. Flow sensors measured peak discharge and infiltration after seasonal rainfall events.

title: Seasonal infiltration in permeable pavement
abstract: Infiltration tests tracked permeable pavement performance across wet and dry seasons. The study compared surface clogging and stormwater runoff in pavement sections with different maintenance schedules.

title: Green roof depth and stormwater retention
abstract: Instrumented green roof plots measured stormwater retention under contrasting substrate depths. Rainfall and runoff records were used to examine whether initial soil moisture explained differences between plots.

title: Distributed bioswales for peak flow reduction
abstract: A neighborhood drainage model evaluated how bioswales changed peak stormwater flow. Observed rainfall and runoff from pilot installations informed estimates of infiltration and downstream discharge.

title: Tree pits as small stormwater storage systems
abstract: Tree pits along a residential street were monitored for rainfall capture and infiltration. The comparison considered how soil compaction and inlet design affected runoff storage during short storms.

title: Acoustic monitoring of birds in urban parks
abstract: Passive acoustic recorders sampled bird activity in urban parks across the breeding season. Detection rates were compared with tree canopy and vegetation structure along standardized survey routes.

title: Pollinator visits in community gardens
abstract: Timed observations counted pollinator visits across community gardens with varied floral diversity. Plant inventories were used to evaluate how seasonal bloom coverage related to bee and butterfly activity.

title: Vegetation corridors and urban bird movement
abstract: Repeated bird surveys along vegetation corridors examined how connectivity and tree canopy related to species detections. Park edges and isolated street trees provided contrasting survey locations.

title: Native plant cover and pollinator diversity
abstract: Garden plots with different native plant cover were surveyed for pollinator diversity. Floral abundance and bloom timing were recorded alongside bee visits to distinguish seasonal patterns.

title: Evening soundscapes at restored wetlands
abstract: Acoustic monitoring captured bird calls and background noise at restored wetlands. The analysis compared detection rates across vegetation zones and evaluated how recording time affected species inventories.

title: Walking access to neighborhood cooling sites
abstract: A pedestrian network model estimated walking access to libraries and other cooling sites. Route shade and daytime heat exposure were included when comparing travel times across residential blocks.
